chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Harun ibn Kharaja, who said:

Indeed, Murad sent a she-camel and ordered that it be yoked and marked on such and such a day. So I said to him, 'It is befitting that he does not wear clothes.' So he sent me to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) in Al-Hira, and I said to him, 'Indeed, Murad did such and such, and he is unable to leave the clothes due to the status of Ziyad.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Instruct him to wear the clothes and let him slaughter a cow on the Day of Eid al-Adha on behalf of himself.'

key_terms.تُشْعَرَ: To be marked with a specific sign or brand
key_terms.تُقَلَّدَ: To be yoked or fitted with a halter
key_terms.زِيَاد: Ziyad (a person, likely a relative or official whose presence/status necessitated wearing clothes)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if one cannot leave their clothes when sending a sacrificial animal?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the principle of ease (taysir) in Shia jurisprudence, where Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) accommodates practical constraints by allowing Murad to wear his clothes during the sacrifice. The ruling introduces a specific compensatory mechanism—slaughtering an additional cow on Eid al-Adha—highlighting the flexibility within the ritual of udhiyah when the ideal conditions cannot be fully met. This reflects the broader Shia scholarly emphasis on adapting legal obligations to the believer's actual capacity without compromising the spiritual intent of the act.
